title: Blessings are tools (9:1)
hookLine: the Torah's promised rewards are means, so we can keep serving
tomorrow: if not for the reward, then why do good at all?

cards: Graduation season brings the envelopes: a check from a grandparent, a laptop from an aunt, sometimes a note tucked inside that says use it well. Maimonides asks a question that turns out to be about those envelopes.
If the real reward for doing good is the world to come, why does the Torah keep promising rain, peace and full barns? Isn't that a second, smaller reward?

teach.b: His answer: the blessings aren't the reward. They're the tools.
God gave the Torah, he says, and promised that if we keep it with joy, the things that block us will be taken away: sickness, war, hunger.
And the things that strengthen our hands will be given: plenty, peace, silver and gold. Why?

teach.h: FREE TO LEARN AND DO GOOD.
teach.b: So that people won't spend all their days on what the body needs, and will be free to learn and to do good. The full barn is a cleared afternoon. The rain is time.
That's the week's question: what is a gift for? And one neighbor answers it in its own words. Christians have a line close to this.
In the New Testament, the first letter of Peter says: "As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God."
A steward holds something that isn't only theirs, to put it to work. The shared thread: what you've been given points past itself. And the honest difference.
Peter's letter speaks of the gifts each person has received, used to serve one another.
Maimonides speaks of the Torah's promised blessings, rain and peace and plenty, as room to learn and keep the commandments on the way to the world to come.
Two traditions, two different books, and one instinct in common: a gift is for using.

how: Jews say blessings over food, new things and good news; Maimonides' reading in 9:1 is taught as the reason the Torah's promises of rain and plenty are means, not the goal.

o: lucky breaks that prove someone has earned favor
the rewards in this life for keeping the commandments
good things given as means to serve, not as the prize

s: Maimonides says rain and plenty are the Torah's reward
they're the tools: they free you to learn and do good, toward the world to come.
his aim is that people not spend all their days on the body's needs
so they're free to learn wisdom and do the commandments.
1 Peter and Maimonides are saying exactly the same thing
both see a gift pointing past itself; Peter means each person's gifts, Maimonides the Torah's blessings.

games.q: you win a month of free groceries in a raffle. what would Maimonides say it's for?
o: enjoy it; it's your reward for being good this year.
the time and money it frees, for learning and doing good.
give it all away at once, so it can't distract you.
games.why: the blessing isn't the prize and isn't a danger. it's room: hours and means freed to learn and do good.

practice: Look at one thing near you that you were given or earned: a phone, a pair of shoes, the chair you're in. Keep your eyes on it for the whole sit. Ask it one question: what are you making room for?
Let whatever answer comes stay with you, without deciding anything yet.

wordCard.voice: Blessings are tools: Maimonides' answer. The Torah's promised rain and peace clear the way to learn and do good.

orig.note: Hebrew: blessing. Maimonides reads the Torah's promised blessings as means.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: blessings are tools, and a gift points past itself. Twenty-three of thirty, carried.

sources.ref: Mishneh Torah, Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) 9:1 (the Torah's promised goods remove what blocks us and strengthen our hands, so we're free to learn wisdom and do the commandments and merit the world to come)
